# The Department of Small Repairs

On the morning the city announced it would be removing the benches, Mara found a teaspoon in her shoe. This was not unprecedented. Her apartment had reached the stage of disorder at which objects migrated without explanation, like birds following magnetic fields. Still, the spoon seemed deliberate. It lay bowl-up inside her left boot, holding a single bead of water. She tipped the water into the sink, put the spoon beside the kettle, and went downstairs to argue with someone.

The notice was attached to the nearest bench with three plastic ties. MUNICIPAL SEATING RATIONALIZATION PROGRAM, it said. Beneath this came a diagram showing the bench replaced by a smooth rectangle of pavement. The projected benefits included improved pedestrian flow, reduced maintenance costs, and fewer undesirable gatherings. A person had underlined “undesirable” in blue ink and written WHO? The bench itself held a sleeping delivery rider, two pigeons, and a woman eating an orange with the concentration of a surgeon.

Mara photographed the notice. Then she sat beside the woman, who offered her a segment of orange without asking whether she wanted one. Across the street, a bakery was raising its shutters. The delivery rider woke, checked his phone, and went back to sleep. “They’re taking it away,” Mara said. The woman nodded toward the notice. “They said that last year.” “Did they?” “They took the other one.” She pointed to a rectangle of newer pavement beside the bus stop.

Mara worked in the Department of Small Repairs, which occupied the third floor of a building nobody could find on their first visit. The entrance faced an alley, though the official address belonged to the street. Its sign had faded until it read DEPARTMENT OF SMALL REPAI S. She had submitted a repair request for the sign twice. The second request was returned because the department was not authorized to repair its own signage without approval from Municipal Identity.

Her duties involved things considered too minor for emergency crews and too public for private responsibility: a handrail loose on three steps, a drinking fountain that sprayed sideways, a pedestrian button that worked only when pressed hard. She liked the work. A repair had an agreeable clarity. Before, the gate scraped the ground. After, it opened. Nobody needed a consultation period to establish whether a gate should open, although recently a consultant had suggested one.

Her supervisor, Mr. Venn, was standing beside the office printer, watching it produce blank pages. “It’s printing,” he said when she arrived. “That’s an improvement.” Mara put the photograph of the bench notice in front of him. He examined it and pushed his glasses higher on his nose. “Public Realm Strategy,” he said. “Not us.” “The bench isn’t broken.” “Then it’s definitely not us.” The printer released another page. He caught it before it joined the white heap on the floor.

Mara asked how a perfectly usable bench could be designated for removal. Mr. Venn opened the shared calendar, as if the answer might be scheduled there. The program had been discussed in February. Small Repairs had not attended; the invitation had gone to a defunct mailbox. “You can ask Strategy,” he said. “But don’t take it personally.” He handed her the morning’s assignments: a tilted litter bin, a broken latch, and a complaint about a mysterious clicking sound near the canal.

The litter bin required two bolts. The latch required oil and patience. The clicking sound came from a man feeding dried peas into the spokes of his bicycle. He said it kept sparrows away from his sandwich. Mara asked whether it worked. He looked at the sparrow standing on his knee and admitted the results were mixed. By lunchtime she had completed her official work and found the seating program online. Forty-seven benches were marked for removal. Her bench was number nineteen.

The assessment gave each bench a score based on surface condition, location, observed usage, and maintenance burden. Number nineteen had received a usage score of zero. Mara looked back at the photograph she had taken that morning. Three people were sitting on it. She scrolled to the assessor’s visit: Tuesday, January 16, 6:10 a.m. That had been the morning of freezing rain, when even the buses stopped on the hills. She printed the page, then wrote a polite email requesting another assessment.

The reply arrived almost immediately. Her message had been received and assigned a reference number. Further correspondence should quote that number. At the bottom, in smaller type, she was advised that submission of correspondence did not constitute grounds for delaying implementation. She read this twice, ate the sandwich she had brought from home, and called the number on the website. A recorded voice thanked her for contributing to a more efficient city. Then the call disconnected.

After work she returned to the bench with a notebook. The orange woman was there again, this time holding a pharmacy bag. Her name was Inez. She lived above the locksmith and came down each afternoon because the staircase tired her and the bench made the walk worthwhile. Mara asked whether she could record how long Inez sat there. “Are you charging?” Inez asked. When Mara explained, she agreed, provided Mara did not describe her as elderly. “Write retired,” she said.

For the next four days, Mara spent her lunch breaks and evenings counting people. A schoolboy tied his shoelaces. A cleaner waited for a lift. Two sisters ate chips from separate paper cones and argued about their father’s birthday. A man in a dark suit sat for eight minutes with his face in his hands, then straightened his tie and left. Mara recorded times but not names. Some people wanted to know what she was doing. Others seemed relieved when she did not ask.

On Friday, rain drove her under the bakery awning. The baker came out carrying a tray of rolls that had split crookedly in the oven. He gave her one and asked about the notebook. When she explained, he fetched a chair from inside. “You can watch from here,” he said. His name was Tomas. He claimed not to care about the bench, but he remembered who had sat on it every morning that week. He also supplied coffee after Mara’s thermos ran out.

She sent her count to Public Realm Strategy: one hundred and thirty-two separate uses over sixteen hours of observation. She attached photographs showing the cracked foot of the bench, which she could repair cheaply, and the bus stop beyond it, which had no seating. This time a person answered. An officer named Calder thanked her for the additional information. Unfortunately, usage was only one component of the evaluation framework. Removal remained scheduled for the following Thursday. Mara asked for the other scores.

Calder sent a spreadsheet. The bench’s principal failing was that it did not match the street’s proposed visual scheme. New seating would be installed at the civic square, seven hundred metres away. Mara walked there during lunch. The square had pale stone paving, six young trees tied to stakes, and a fountain that ran on alternate days. The new seats were attractive. She sat on one and watched an office worker carefully arrange a folded jacket between his back and the metal support.

She returned to her office and asked Mr. Venn whether replacing a cracked bench foot required permission from Strategy. “Ordinarily, no,” he said. “But you know it’s coming out.” “Until it comes out, it’s a public asset with a reported defect.” He looked at her for a while, then requested the photograph. The crack was real, and the repair was within their budget. He signed the work order. “No speeches,” he said. “Repair it, photograph it, close the job.”

On Monday morning Mara arrived with a toolbox, a steel brace, and two bags of quick-setting concrete. Her colleague Dev came with her. He had offered to help without asking why she was so interested in this particular bench. They lifted one end, cleaned the damaged foot, and bolted on the brace. Inez watched from the bakery chair. The delivery rider, whose name was Leon, held a spirit level against the seat. By ten, the bench stood squarely for the first time in years.

While the concrete cured, Tomas put a handwritten sign on it: PLEASE DO NOT SIT UNTIL NOON. Someone crossed out NOON and wrote FREE. Someone else added a smile. Mara removed the altered sign and made another. She had no wish to submit a photograph of a repaired public asset apparently advertising free sitting. Dev laughed, but he helped her clean the old paint drips off the slats. Underneath, they found initials, a date, and a shallow groove where somebody had worked patiently with a key.

At noon they took away the barrier. Inez sat first. She tested the bench by shifting her weight, then pronounced it better. Mara photographed the repaired foot and returned to the office to close the job. Before she did, she sent the photograph to Calder, along with the new maintenance cost: forty-three pounds and twenty pence. Calder replied that the repair was appreciated but had no bearing on the removal decision. Mara stared at “appreciated” until Mr. Venn asked whether she was going home.

On Tuesday, Inez brought an envelope containing seven signatures from her building. Tomas had collected twenty-three from customers. Leon sent Mara a message from a rider’s group, where nine people said they used the bench between deliveries. Mara had not asked any of them to do this. She spent the evening putting their comments into one document, keeping the spelling as written. At midnight she removed a paragraph of her own explaining why benches mattered. The comments were more useful.

On Wednesday Calder called. The residents’ submission had been forwarded by two councillors and needed a response. He could meet Mara at the site at three. She asked whether the removal would be paused. He could not promise that. At three he arrived wearing a coat too light for the weather, carrying a folder under one arm. He was younger than Mara expected and looked tired. For a moment they both stood beside the bench, uncertain how to begin without sounding hostile.

Inez settled the matter by asking Calder to sit down. He did. She described the journey from her flat to the pharmacy: thirty-one stairs, a crossing, a stretch without shop doorways where she could rest. The civic square was in the wrong direction. Calder took notes. Leon arrived and explained that the nearest café required a purchase and closed before his last shift. Tomas brought coffee, including one for Calder, who accepted it with both hands. Mara stayed standing. She had already said plenty.

Calder opened his folder. The removal contract covered all forty-seven benches, and changing it would incur a charge. The visual scheme had been approved. There were complaints about late-night noise at several locations. “Here?” Mara asked. He checked. Not here. The assessment had grouped benches by street rather than by site. He looked at the repaired foot, then asked for a copy of the work order. Mara emailed it while he watched. He said he would make a recommendation, but the crew might still arrive tomorrow.

They did, at eight fifteen. Mara was there because she had slept badly and left home early. A flatbed truck stopped beside the curb. Two workers got out and checked a tablet. One laid a socket wrench on the bench while the other photographed it. Mara introduced herself, gave her department, and asked whether they had received a revised instruction. They had not. The older worker, Bell, showed her the screen. Bench nineteen, removal authorized. He was friendly but clearly expected an argument.

Mara called Calder. No answer. She called his office and was transferred twice, eventually reaching someone who said he was in a briefing. Behind her, the bakery shutter rose. Inez appeared at her doorway in slippers, saw the truck, and went back inside for shoes. Bell waited while Mara called Mr. Venn. “I can’t stop their job,” Venn said. “Send me the contract reference.” She did. He told her not to stand in front of the truck. She had not considered it until then.

By eight thirty, seven people had gathered. Nobody shouted. Tomas brought a tray of coffee and asked the crew whether they wanted breakfast. The younger worker accepted; Bell checked his watch. They had another eleven removals to complete. Inez sat on the bench and opened her newspaper. Leon arrived carrying a bicycle wheel that needed replacing. He leaned it against the repaired foot. It was a small, awkward assembly, with no banner and no clear plan beyond making the removal take longer.

At eight forty-two, Bell’s phone rang. He listened, looked at the bench, and asked the caller to repeat the instruction. Then he picked up his wrench. “Leave this one pending review,” he said to his colleague. Mara felt so relieved she almost thanked him for something he had not decided. Instead, she thanked both workers for waiting. Bell drank his coffee standing up. Before getting into the truck, he told Inez she could close her newspaper now. She said she had been reading it.

The review lasted six weeks. During that time Mara learned more about procurement than she had ever wanted to know. Retaining one bench required a revised asset record, a small contract adjustment, and an exception to the visual scheme. Calder asked her department to confirm responsibility for future maintenance. Mr. Venn agreed, then sent Mara a private message: This is not an invitation to adopt all forty-seven. She promised nothing. There were eleven other benches whose usage scores looked suspiciously low.

Bench nineteen stayed. Three others stayed too, after residents challenged their assessments. Twenty-nine were removed, seven were relocated, and seven received another review. Mara could not call the outcome a victory without thinking of the places she had not visited. Nor was it nothing. On the morning the final decision arrived, she took her usual route downstairs and found Inez sharing the bench with a boy whose schoolbag occupied almost as much space as he did. They moved the bag so Mara could sit.

Autumn brought smaller jobs. A door closer needed adjusting at the library. The canal path acquired a loose railing. Someone reported that the repaired bench had a splinter on the backrest. Mara sanded it down and sealed the patch before rain could get into the wood. Leon passed while she worked and stopped to tell her he had found a better delivery route. Tomas tapped on his window to ask whether she wanted coffee. She held up one finger: a minute.

That evening she cleaned her apartment. Under the bed she found two socks, a receipt from the winter, and the missing cap from a jar of cumin. The teaspoon was still beside the kettle. She washed it and put it in the drawer, where it fitted among the others. Then she made tea and sat by the open window. Downstairs, somebody laughed. A bus stopped, lowered itself toward the curb, and waited while a passenger boarded. Mara drank her tea before it cooled.
